How FLOSS works

Source: vignettes/floss-00-how-it-works.Rmd
floss-00-how-it-works.Rmd

This guide describes the model, the treatments, the sampling and what to expect in the data. The same text will be the Guide tab of the app. For worked examples see vignette("floss-02-user-guide") and vignette("floss-03-teaching").

1. What FLOSS does

FLOSS simulates fisheries whose truth is known and the data they produce. It is built for teaching: trainees predict how a stock responds to a change, see the response in the true dynamics and in the data, and learn to recognise warning flags, patterns in data that real dynamics cannot produce.

A FLOSS run has five layers:

  1. Fishery: fleets, years and nominal effort, shared by all species.
  2. Species: life history, target MSY, selectivity and catchability by fleet.
  3. Operating model (OM): the true age-structured dynamics.
  4. Sampling: the data an observer would collect (catch, effort, CPUE, survey, length samples, biological samples).
  5. Truth and export: one dataset per iteration, with a separate answer key.

A treatment changes one thing in the OM (F, recruitment, selectivity, creep, M) and is run against an untreated baseline with the same random numbers, so every difference comes from the treatment.

FLOSS describes dynamics and data. Fitting assessment models to the data (e.g. with FLicc or JABBA) follows afterwards, using the exported data and the answer key to judge the results.

2. Fishery and effort

Each fleet has a nominal effort trend, E[f, y], with lognormal process noise that is shared by all species: when a fleet fishes more in a year, it fishes more on every species it catches. Effort creep raises the efficiency of a fleet by a constant percentage per year; it increases fishing mortality but is not visible in the nominal effort index.

F[s, f, y] = relq[s, f] x Fmsy[s] x efficiency[f, y] x E[f, y]

In the app, choose New fishery to start with no gears, add gears by name and set each gear’s effort; species get a default selectivity for a new gear (S-shaped at the length at maturity) to be set in the Species step. In R, fishery() takes any fleet names and species() a selectivity and catchability for each.

relq is the relative catchability of species s by fleet f, set in the species. With one fleet and one_gear_species(), effort equals F/Fmsy.

3. Species

A species holds von Bertalanffy growth (linf, k, t0), the length-weight relationship (a, b; cm and g), maturity (lm, tm), maximum age (also the plus group), natural mortality M, steepness s, recruitment variability sigR, a target MSY, and selectivity and relative catchability by fleet. Selectivity is defined on length (logistic, normal or double normal) and converted to age through growth.

The four example species (Siganus sutor, Lethrinus mahsena, Lutjanus bohar, Carcharhinus melanopterus) are read-only; copies can be saved to the user’s species library.

4. Operating model

The OM is an age-structured model built with FLR:

  • the equilibrium is calibrated so that MSY equals the target (the unfished biomass is rescaled);
  • fleet F-at-age is apical F times fleet selectivity; total F is the sum over fleets;
  • the stock is projected with Beverton-Holt recruitment and lognormal deviations (optionally autocorrelated);
  • reference points (Fmsy, Bmsy, MSY, B0) are recomputed for the realised fleet mix of the last years.

The equilibrium curves (yield, SSB and recruitment against F) describe where the stock would settle under constant fishing. The realised years usually lie off these curves: during a fishing-down phase, catches exceed the equilibrium yield because biomass is being removed; after a reduction in F the stock takes years to rebuild.

5. Treatments

Treatment What changes Typical lesson
F step (effort) effort of a fleet x mult from a year lags: biomass and length structure respond over years
Fleet leaves (effort, mult = 0) one fleet stops other fleets’ indicators and the fleet mix change
Recruitment pulse recruitment x mult in some years a cohort moves through the length data; catches rise later
Recruitment trend or regime recruitment declines or shifts mean length rises while the stock declines
Selectivity change a fleet’s gear changes from a year length data and catch curves change without a change in F
Effort creep efficiency rises from a year CPUE stays high while the stock declines
M change natural mortality x mult productivity and reference points change

Baseline and treated runs share every random number (effort noise, recruitment deviations, sampling). Before the treatment year they are identical.

6. Sampling

Data How it is generated Key settings
Catch by fleet true catch x (1 - under-reporting) x lognormal error CV, bias, bias from year
Effort index nominal effort x lognormal error CV
CPUE by fleet vulnerable biomass^beta x efficiency (if creep is carried) x lognormal AR1 error CV, rho, beta, catchability step
Survey index biomass at survey time x survey selectivity, AR1 error timing, CV, rho, selectivity (relative to Linf), catchability step
Length samples two-stage sampling by season: clusters drawn from the season’s catch-at-age, then fish measured through the gear’s length key at the middle of the season clusters (ess_age), fish measured (ess_len), length bin, seasonal design
Biological samples one row per fish and season: length (mm), age (with ageing error and bias), weight (g), maturity (0/1) fish per year, ageing scheme (random or length-stratified), CVs, seasonal design

CPUE, length and biological samples cover the last years of each fleet (e.g. 5, 10 and 15 years in the reef example); catch and effort cover all years.

Two-stage length sampling. Fish in a trip or haul are alike, so a length sample carries less information than its number of fish suggests. The effective sample size lies between the number of clusters and the number of fish measured, depending on growth and selectivity.

Seasonal sampling. The stock is annual, with fishing effort spread evenly through the year; only the sampling is seasonal. By default the length and biological samples of a year are spread evenly over four seasons (season_design()). Within a season the catch-at-age is the catch taken between the start and end of the season, and lengths are those at the middle of the season, so fish in late-season samples are larger. Imbalanced designs:

Design Example Effect on the pooled annual length data
Balanced equal shares none
Fixed imbalance most samples in season 1 mean length too low every year (a constant bias)
Shift sampling moves to seasons 3 and 4 from 2018 a step in mean length in 2018 that looks like a change in mortality
Opportunistic shares vary at random from year to year extra year-to-year noise in mean length
Missing season share 0 in the monsoon no information on that part of the year
Gradual shift the shift spread over several years a slow drift in mean length, easily read as a trend in the stock
Fewer samples sample size x 0.3 from 2020 (funding cut) noisier length data, more erratic indicators
Missing years each year unsampled with some probability gaps; cohorts harder to follow

lfd_annual(weight = "equal") and length_indicators(season_weight = "equal") give every sampled season the same weight, which corrects an uneven spread but cannot recover a season that was not sampled. plot_seasons() shows the sample sizes and the mean length by season.

Autocorrelated CPUE residuals. A fleet that keeps fishing the same grounds does not sample the stock at random; its errors persist from year to year (rho > 0), so each year adds less independent information.

7. Size data: what to expect

At equilibrium (constant recruitment and mortality, flat-topped selectivity) a length composition has a fixed shape:

  • the ascending limb is set by selectivity (Lc, the length of first capture);

  • the descending limb is set by mortality relative to growth, Z/k;

  • mean length above Lc follows Beverton and Holt (1956):

    Lmean = (Linf + (Z/k) Lc) / (1 + Z/k)    so    Z = k (Linf - Lmean) / (Lmean - Lc)

Heavier fishing gives a lower mean length, a shorter right-hand tail and fewer large fish (lower L95, Pmega).

What breaks the pattern:

Violation What the length data show Misread as Clue
F has just changed mean length adjusts over years F still high (or low) indicators still trending
Strong cohort a mode enters small and moves right first overfishing, then recovery the mode moves at the growth rate; other indices show the year class
Recruitment declining fewer small fish, mean length rises recovery juvenile index and CPUE fall
Recruitment rising more small fish, mean length falls overfishing juvenile index rises
Dome-shaped gear large fish missing whatever F high F a logistic gear or the survey still sees large fish
Gear or target change step in length composition sudden change in F coincides with a fleet event
Low effective sample size erratic year-to-year shapes recruitment variation consecutive years not consistent with growth

Real modes move to the right by about one year’s growth per year, fade at rate Z, and appear in every gear that can catch them. Patterns that jump, vanish or appear in one gear only are sampling noise or selectivity.

8. Warning flags

Flag in the data Likely cause, not real dynamics
CPUE flat or rising while survey, catch and mean length decline effort creep or hyperstable CPUE
Catch well above MSY for years with no decline in any index over-reported catch, or indices that do not track abundance
Mean length rises while F rises dome-shaped gear or a gear change
Catch-curve Z below M selectivity not flat on the descending limb, or a recruitment trend
A strong year class in an index that never moves through the length data index noise or ageing error
A step in an index in one year change in catchability (vessel, gear, electronics)
A step in mean length in the year the sampling season changed seasonal sampling shift (fish are larger later in the year)
CPUE residuals running in long streaks non-random sampling
CPUE of a gear that catches juveniles (or lets large fish escape) declines much less than other indices the gear’s vulnerable biomass is not the spawning stock (see plot_ssb_vb())

Plausibility checks: a stock cannot grow faster than its productivity allows; cohorts must move through lengths at the growth rate; biomass does not respond to F instantly; and independent indicators of the same stock should broadly agree. When they do not, at least one of them is not tracking the stock.

9. Truth and export

export_data() writes one folder (or workbook) per iteration with the observed data and a README, plus a separate answer_key/ folder with the true time series, reference points, true status, true catch, true ages and the list of planted artefacts (data problems and treatments set on purpose). Remove the answer key before giving the data to trainees. export_truth() writes the truth alone, for the trainer.

Naive aggregation (teaching). Effort is reported in fishing days, so catch, effort and nominal CPUE (kg per fishing day) can be summed over fleets, or over fleets and species (catch_table(), effort_table(), nominal_cpue(), plot_aggregate()), and length samples pooled over fleets as measured or raised to each fleet’s catch (lfd_aggregate()). Biological samples can be grouped by fleet, all fleets or season (plot_bio(by =)). export_data(aggregate = TRUE) adds these tables to the export.

Aggregate What it ignores What it can produce
Effort summed over fleets a fishing day differs between gears effort that rises while F falls (fleet mix)
Nominal CPUE, all fleets fleet catchability and selectivity trends driven by the fleet mix
Nominal CPUE, all species species composition a stable index while one species collapses
Length samples pooled as measured catch share of each fleet the most sampled fleet dominates

FLR objects. as_flr() and export_data(format = "rds") give FLQuants of catch, effort and length frequencies, FLIndices with log-scale SEs and the life-history FLPar, ready for JABBA3 (jb3_data()) and FLicc (stocklen(), fiticc()).
